newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea's trade deficit cut sparks new hope.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's trade deficit cut sparks new hope.

text.p: South Korea's merchandise trade deficit shrank in April, and the first good news on the trade front this year sparked cautious optimism that an economic slump may be bottoming out.
The trade ministry said on Thursday the customs-cleared trade deficit narrowed to $1.5 billion in April from a $2.04 billion shortfall a year earlier.
"This is the first month the trade deficit has narrowed year-on-year since the beginning of this year," the ministry said.
The deficit also eased from a shortfall of $1.85 billion in March, $2.14 billion in February and $3.49 billion in January.
"The trade balance will continue to improve throughout this year on exports recovery and slowing imports," said Lee Keun-tae, an economist at LG Economic Research Institute.
"The trade deficit is expected to reach $14 billion this year, down considerably from a $20.6 billion shortfall last year."
Lee's projection exactly matches the trade ministry's forecast of a $14 billion deficit this year.
But Rhee Namuh, a research head of Dongbang Peregrine Securities, was less optimistic.
"An improvement is seen this year but not as much as the government thinks," he said.
The ballooning trade deficit has been the main factor dragging on economic growth. South Korea's gross domestic product is forecast to grow at six percent this year against 7.1 percent in 1996.
Export growth of 7.0 percent in April was the first monthly rise for 1997. Exports posted negative growth in January to March.
"Moreover, this is the first time since last June that export growth has outpaced import growth," the ministry said.
Imports gained a mere 1.6 percent last month.

Semiconductor sales abroad fell 14.2 percent in April due to a plunge in chip prices, the ministry said. Prices of 16 megabit dynamic random access memory (DRAM) chips stood at $8.50 to $10.00 last month from $22.30 a year earlier.
But exports excluding computer chips rose 10.5 percent.
Oil product exports surged 34.9 percent, while steel products gained 24.7 percent and automobiles 11.6 percent.
"The ministry forecasts exports to grow in the near future, buoyed by a recovery in exports of petrochemicals, automobiles, steel products and textile goods," the ministry said.
"Steady improvement in the trade balance is expected as imports of capital goods are unlikely to rise for the time being, and global crude oil prices are forecast to remain stable for quite a while."
Analysts said prices of South Korea's major export items, including semiconductors, steel products and petrochemical products, had stopped falling for the time being.
"For two to three months, we'll see a recovery in exports on improvement in prices of DRAMs, steel and chemicals," said Rhee of Dongbang Peregrine.
"But it could get difficult in the second half due to a possibility that chemicals and steel could face regional oversupply."
Import growth is expected to slow this year, depressed by an overall economic downturn, analysts and economists said.
Imports of capital goods fell 0.6 percent in April, while consumer goods imports rose 1.5 percent on a drop in overseas grain purchases.
"A slowdown in imports, not export expansion, could be the engine behind a fall in the trade deficit," said Lee of LG.
